title: Also the CGI is bad but that’s an industry-wide problem 🤷🏻‍♂️ #wicked...
transcript: I used to argue with people about whether Wicked has a happy ending. For context, a lot of my middle school classmates and I first saw Wicked at roughly the same time, because it came to our hometown. I said I found the ending extremely sad, that it made me cry. But my un-extraordinary classmates were not as emotionally intelligent as I was at age 13. So naturally, they said, “what do you mean? it wasn't sad!” “Elphaba lives in the end!” So I said, “ugh, media literacy is dead!” And I took a sip from my scotch on the rocks, and I reminded them that the living carry heavier burdens than the dead. Wicked is a devastating tragedy, actually, because it's the story of two friends torn apart, one fleeing an exile, the other one burdened with unimaginable guilt for the rest of her life. Anyway, I finally saw Wicked For Good this week, and I'm a little surprised it's getting such negative reception, because on the whole, I thought it had a lot of the same strengths and weaknesses as part 1. And as a lot of people have pointed out, many of the places where it's weaker have more to do with act two of the musical being weaker than Act one. Like, sure,there are moments in this movie that I thought were executed in a pretty clumsy or awkward way, not least of which the two new songs, which I found incredibly flat and uninspired. But just as often I'd say to myself “hmm, that was a little stupid” and then realize “wait, that's exactly how it's written in the show “and I just never thought about it.” Granted, that's not necessarily a good excuse. If something doesn't work, it doesn't work. And a truly great adaptation would improve on the weak points of the source material. But I do think it does that in some areas. And conversely, Part 1 has its fair share of fumbled moments too. As listless and forgettable as the new songs are in part 2, nothing in either movie made me cringe as hard as the part they added for Idina and Kristin. Can we reopen this case, please? And while I think both movies benefited somewhat from being fleshed out over a longer run time, I criticized part 1 for going a little too far in that direction, whereas part 2 split the difference a little better for me, even if it had a slightly messier feel to it. At the end of the day, I enjoyed both movies because I think they're united by what I consider to be their most important shared strength, which is fleshing out the world and the story while keeping their finger firmly planted on the pulse of what makes it emotionally resonant: the beautifully tragic relationship between Elphaba and Glinda. And a case could be made that emphasizing the passage of time allows their journey to carry even more weight. And Likewise, with a larger sense of scope and context, the rifts that tear them apart cut all the deeper, so much so that even the average middle schooler would be hard-pressed to leave the theatre unmoved.
